scoreNote: Guest states 'we do own some OpenAI' and 'I am bullish on OpenAI' — confirmed long position with explicit bull thesis.
summary: Thomas Lafont is bullish on OpenAI, citing ChatGPT's dominant 80%+ market share, 300 million weekly actives, over a million enterprise users, and its compounding personalization advantage, which he views as evidence of a dominant, fast-growing franchise worth owning.
quote: I am bullish on OpenAI... it is maintaining 80% plus market share... I think the ChatGPT franchise inside of OpenAI is one of the great most successful, fastest growing kind of stories.

scoreNote: Guest confirms existing investment in TikTok/ByteDance and provides a forward-looking valuation thesis.
summary: Thomas Lafont, as an existing investor in ByteDance, argues TikTok's US asset is an incredibly valuable franchise worth roughly $100 billion, based on time-spent parity with Meta despite half the DAUs, though regulatory and deal uncertainty make precise valuation difficult.
quote: We are investors in TikTok... is $100 billion a reasonable scenario? You know, I think the math proves it... it's an incredibly valuable franchise.

summary: Chamath believes TikTok's US asset, while intrinsically worth ~$100 billion, will transact at a much lower price approaching zero because the US government controls its ability to exist, making the government the effectively unconstrained price-setter in any deal.
quote: I believe it. I do think it's about a $100 billion asset. But at the end of the day, the president was very clear that it is completely and entirely worthless without his permit... I find it very hard to see how it gets to the actual value

scoreNote: Jason explicitly states he is a shareholder and is 'delighted' with performance — confirmed long.
summary: Jason notes he is a Netflix shareholder and is pleased with its subscriber performance and stock price appreciation, viewing recent results as validation of a working strategy.
quote: I am a shareholder and I am delighted. I don't know what's going on over there, but they seem to be getting their subs right... there's some strategy that's working over there.

summary: Chamath acknowledges Netflix is a well-run, performant business but frames its success as a negative social indicator — a 'sink for people's time' correlated with declining labor participation and rising depression rates — without making a directional investment call.
quote: It's obviously a very good company. I think it's been incredibly performant, but I think it has a little bit of a dark commentary on American society and productivity.

summary: Thomas Lafont highlights Constellation Energy as an interesting public market idea, noting that Amazon and Microsoft are signing direct behind-the-meter power deals with the company and that even the Biden administration contracted with CEG, signaling broad recognition that nuclear is the best path forward for AI data center power.
quote: I don't know if you guys have been following this stock in the public market, guys, called Constellation Energy. Oh yeah, it's a really interesting idea. What's interesting of what Amazon and Microsoft is, they're actually signing deals

summary: Chamath flags Broadcom as a massively underappreciated trillion-dollar company built through disciplined M&A roll-ups, noting it rarely gets the attention of peers like Nvidia or Meta despite its scale.
quote: It is the only trillion-dollar company that nobody talks about. Everybody knows Nvidia, everybody knows Amazon, Meta, but Broadcom is a $1. $1, $2 trillion business. And it started basically through a whole series of roll-ups.

summary: Thomas Lafont characterizes Intel's dramatic underperformance relative to Broadcom and Nvidia as a complete abdication of corporate governance at both the board and CEO level, implying structural failure rather than cyclical weakness.
quote: I think Intel really missed. It's a complete abdication of corporate governance at the board level and the CEO level.

summary: Guest (Thomas) makes a bullish case for uranium, citing the inevitability of nuclear energy growth to power AI and compete with China, noting they buy uranium and expect the trend toward nuclear to continue over the next 10-20 years.
quote: Why we buy uranium? I think you can speak to that better... we expect, and we think just the trend generally towards nuclear energy is going to continue... I think it will show to be a part of the AI kind of arms race, you know, over the next 10, 20 years.

summary: Friedberg is bullish on uranium/nuclear, arguing Gen 4 reactor technology makes nuclear viable and safe, that China is massively scaling while the US deploys zero, and that the US must urgently act or face severe energy and AI competitiveness disadvantages.
quote: China's rolling out dozens or hundreds of these, and the United States is rolling out zero, and that needs to change... we only have a couple of months to get the engine stood up that will allow us to make the material... to actually deploy these stations to try and have a shot at catching up.
